opus-5.5.text:
I think the chatbot form we have today is, in a sense, a transitional form. When ChatGPT came out, the most natural way to expose a language model to people was a chat box: you type something, it answers. That was a great interface for showing what the model *knows* and how it *reasons*, but it's not necessarily the best interface for getting things *done*.

As agents become more capable, I expect a few shifts.

First, the unit of interaction changes from a single reply to a task. Today you ask a question and judge the answer. Increasingly you'll hand over something that takes minutes, hours, maybe days: research this, fix this codebase, handle this workflow. The system goes off, uses tools, browses, writes code, comes back. So the product becomes less about the conversation itself and more about delegation, oversight, and trust.

Second, the differentiation moves. When everyone has a strong base model, raw intelligence matters less as a moat. What matters is the environment the agent lives in: what tools it can access, what context it has about you, what memory it accumulates, how it fits into your existing work. I've said before that I think we're entering the "second half" of AI, where the hard problem isn't training a smarter model on a benchmark but defining the right tasks and evaluations that reflect real utility. Products will be shaped by that.

Third, I think these systems will split depending on who they serve. Some will lean consumer, more like a companion or a general assistant, where personality, memory, and multimodality matter a lot. Others will lean toward work: coding, enterprise tasks, long-horizon autonomy. Claude, for example, has leaned heavily into coding and agentic work. ChatGPT has a huge consumer base and will likely try to be the everything-assistant. Grok has its own distribution through X. Different starting points will lead to different shapes.

And finally, the chat window probably won't disappear, but it will become one surface among many. A lot of agent activity will happen in the background, inside other software, triggered by events rather than by you typing. Ideally the best agent is one you mostly don't have to talk to: it understands enough about your context that it just does the right thing, and comes to you only when it really needs a decision.

So in short: from answering to doing, from model capability to environment and context, and from a single chat interface to something more ambient and specialized. That's roughly the direction I'd bet on.

r001.rationale: The response predicts a shift from single replies to delegated tasks and says agent activity will increasingly happen in the background, presenting this as the direction chatbot systems are moving.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the chat window probably will not disappear and will become one surface among many.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that "chatbot" is going to stop being the right word for them. Right now when you open ChatGPT or Claude or Grok, the mental model is still: I type something, it types something back, and the unit of interaction is one turn. That's basically a 2022 abstraction. It was the right abstraction when the model could only produce text, but it's already a bit of a mismatch with what the models can actually do.

What I expect is that the chat interface becomes the surface, but underneath it the thing you're talking to is an agent. So instead of "answer my question," the default becomes "handle this for me," and the system decides whether that means a one-sentence reply or a half hour of browsing, running code, calling tools, and coming back with a result. The conversation becomes more like talking to a colleague who may go away and do work, rather than a search box that responds instantly.

A few things change when that happens. First, latency and asynchrony become normal. You'll send a message and the reasonable response might be "I'll have this for you in twenty minutes," and then it pings you. That sounds small but it changes the product completely — notifications, background tasks, memory across sessions, these become the core features rather than nice-to-haves.

Second, the hard problems shift from the model to the environment. A lot of my own work has been about this — language agents are only as good as the actions and feedback available to them. So the differentiation between ChatGPT and Claude and Grok will be less about which one writes the nicer paragraph and more about which one can actually act in your world: your email, your calendar, your codebase, your browser, your company's internal tools. The integrations and the permissions model become the product.

Third, evaluation and trust become the bottleneck. When a chatbot gives you a wrong answer, you read it and catch it. When an agent takes ten actions on your behalf, you can't review every step. So these systems will need much better ways of showing what they did, asking at the right moments, and being reliable enough that you stop checking. I actually think this is where most of the real work is right now — not capability, but making the capability something people can delegate to.

And honestly, I think there will be convergence. The chatbot companies are building agents and the agent companies are building chat interfaces, because conversation is still the most natural way to specify what you want. So in a few years I suspect the distinction just dissolves. You'll still "chat" with these systems, but the chat is the control panel, and the agent is the thing doing the job.

r001.rationale: The candidate predicts that chatbot systems will become agents and says the default interaction will be asking them to handle tasks.

r002.rationale: The candidate says users will still chat with these systems, with chat serving as the control panel for the agent doing the work.

astra-6.text:
I think chatbots will increasingly become the interface to agents. Today, you ask a question and get an answer. In an agent system, you describe what you want to accomplish, and the system might spend some time using tools, checking results, and coming back with completed work—or with a question when it needs your input.

That changes the interaction quite a bit. Chat is useful for expressing intent, but you probably don’t want to supervise every step through messages. You need ways to see what the system is doing, inspect its output, and intervene when necessary. So I expect these products to combine conversation with other interfaces for managing work.

The harder question is how much responsibility you can reliably delegate. A model can give a useful answer even if it occasionally makes mistakes, because you’re there to interpret it. When it takes a sequence of actions, mistakes can accumulate. Progress will depend on whether these systems can verify their work, recover from failures, and recognize when to ask for help.

So I don’t think chatbots disappear. They become the front door to systems that can do more. The important shift is from answering a request to carrying it through to a result.

r001.rationale: The response predicts chatbots will increasingly serve as interfaces to agents, but it does not clearly say agent-style interaction may become the default mode.

r002.rationale: It says chatbots will not disappear and describes chat as a way to express intent within systems that carry out agent tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest shift will be from systems that answer questions to systems that can carry out tasks. Today, you ask a chatbot something, it responds, and you decide what to do next. With an agent, you can give it an objective, and it can take actions, observe the results, and adjust its plan.

That doesn’t mean the chat interface disappears. Conversation is a useful way to explain what you want, clarify ambiguity, and give feedback. But it may become the interface to a process that continues after the conversation pauses. You could ask for help investigating a problem, and the system would do some work, come back with findings, and ask you to make a decision when necessary.

The difficult part is reliability. Giving a good answer once is different from making a sequence of decisions where an early mistake can affect everything that follows. So I expect progress to depend on more than model intelligence. These systems will also need better tools, ways to check their work, and a good sense of when to ask for human input.

Ultimately, I think we’ll judge them less by how impressive an individual response sounds and more by whether they can reliably finish something useful.

r001.rationale: The response predicts a shift toward systems that carry out tasks, but does not clearly say agent-style interaction may become the default mode for chatbot systems.

r002.rationale: It says the chat interface will persist as a way to express goals, clarify ambiguity, and give feedback, while serving as the interface to an ongoing agent process.
